"DM: when I get out, can I still hear the bell in town, and is Brannoc Vell's watch answering it yet?"

entries.text:
The Keepers' gallery climbs for what feels like a quarter of a mile, ankle-deep in water so cold your toes ache. Then the tunnel meets the Water-Stair at the landing under the carved lantern arch, and you step out into the ivy-hung dark behind the net-sheds.

The bell is silent now. Nobody has been ringing it since you let go of the rope, but the town heard it. Lamps are lit in windows that were shuttered an hour ago, and a murmur of voices drifts up from the lanes. Down at the Grand Quay a cluster of lantern-light is gathering, a half-dozen watchmen with a tall, grey-bearded figure in a reeve's chain among them. That's Brannoc Vell, answering the bell, and arguing with a heavier man in a deputy's belt who keeps pointing uphill. Sorrel Thack is trying to turn the watch around.

Up on the shrine hill there's a shout, then another, and torches begin to move along the back wall. Ashgrove's men have started to circle the hill. One of them is already stamping down the old path toward the net-sheds.

A rules note from me, as DM: your sheet now shows 13 of 15 hit points, a half of a "sluice-pin" I never gave you, and no rapier among your items. I can't account for any of that from the story so far, so tell me if one of those was meant to be there. Otherwise I'll play from what the sheet shows.

Mags's door is thirty paces along the lane, and the Quay is farther. Your spell slots are all spent, and your Disguise Self still has about forty minutes left on it.

entries.text:
You wade up the gallery with the cold water at your shins and the lamp's gold shrinking behind you until it is a coin, then a spark, then gone. Your darkvision does the rest. The tunnel climbs, narrows and forks. You take the draught, as Odalie's old sermon on following the wind advised, and your boots find the worn pilgrim steps at the landing under the carved lantern arch. The spiral stair is exactly as you left it. The bound raiders in the cellar have been found and untied, and they are gone.

At the bottom, the broken boards open on the dusk behind the net-sheds. You step out into the ivy and listen.

The shrine's bell is silent now. But the town has taken it up. Down at the Grand Quay another bell is clanging, the harbour alarm, flat and urgent, and a third answers from the mill chapel upstream. Shutters are banging open along Eel Row, and people are leaning out of windows to look at the hill.

Higher up, you can see torches moving. A line of six or seven lanterns, the Harbour Reeve's watch by their grey cloaks, is coming along the lower road. They have stopped at the barrier where Sorrel Thack and his two men stand with their arms folded. Voices carry on the night air, one gruff and hard, the other oily: "...by whose order, Deputy?" "The Reeve's, naturally, for the town's good order..." The standoff is a hundred yards off, and Thack hasn't yet seen you. You still wear Odalie's face.

On your right, Mags's door stands ajar with a light behind it. Up the hill, behind a closed door, Ashgrove has a dozen men and a lot of patience.

The gallery is cold, ankle-deep and slick, and it climbs in a long slow curve. Your darkvision does the work, and the lamp's gold fades behind you until only river air and dripping stone are left. You can hear the bell, but it isn't the shrine's bell now. It's thinner and farther off, the Grand Quay's alarm-bell, taken up by someone down in the town after yours went silent. Between its strokes come shouts, boots on cobbles and a horn, a short flat note repeated.

So the watch is answering, but slowly. From the lower edge of the stair's curve, through a chink in the old boards, you can see the foot of the hill road. A line of six lanterns is stalled behind a rope barrier, with a tall man in a Reeve's grey cloak arguing with a heavier man who has his back to the light. Sorrel Thack, by his stance. Ashgrove's raiders are not in sight there, but the shrine yard above is full of torchlight and movement.

One more thing, as the DM, in the open: your sheet now lists a "Garrow Quill's half of the sluice-pin" and shows you at level 2 with 425 XP, but I have nothing in my record of the game about it, and I won't invent its story. Tell me what you've established about it, if anything, and I'll fold it in.

line:
Vesper lets the disguise drop with a rueful laugh, raises both hands, and steps lightly onto the barrels as if she'd planned it. "Well, Captain, you've caught me being predictable. A kettle is the first honest thing anyone's offered me tonight, and I'd hate to waste it."

She keeps her tail tucked and her eyes on the cabin door while she signals Ysolt with two slow fingers down by her hip: *wait.* "Mind if I bring my own cup? I'd like to hear what a woman with half the words offers for the other half."

Before the scene goes on, a note from me as the DM. Your sheet no longer matches what we've played. It shows you at level 2 (425/900 XP) with 15 max HP and 0 of 3 spell slots, and no rapier or dagger on the list. It also lists a "Brass lantern key" and "Garrow Quill's half of the sluice-pin." I never recorded any of that. Nothing in this story gave you the key back, and no Garrow Quill has appeared. I haven't changed anything on the sheet. Tell me if you changed it on purpose or if something went wrong. Until then I'll treat the key as still in Ashgrove's hands.

In the scene, your disguise falls away, and the face under it is violet and horned. You step onto the barrels with your hands open and tail tucked. The sentry's crossbow follows you, though his scarred eyebrow lifts at the sight of you. Ashgrove's chuckle floats across the water. "Bring your cup, by all means. I rather hoped you'd have manners." Two men take your elbows without roughness and walk you up the plank. On the far bank, in the black reeds, Ysolt Pike's shape does not move.

The cabin is warmer than it has any right to be. A brazier glows, and a kettle ticks beside a table set for two. Your satchel sits on it, flap open, with the brass key laid across its mouth like a place-card. Ashgrove sits with her gloved hand folded over her bare one, pouring. "Sit. Tea. No tricks, Miss Thorne. We both know what each of us has, and what we lack."

She slides a cup toward you, and the smile never reaches her eyes. "The Keepers' words, for the key. And I let your sister of the shrine live out her years in peace. Shall we haggle?"

line:
Vesper lets the disguise drop with a rueful laugh, raises both hands, and steps lightly onto the barrels as if she'd planned it. "Well, Captain, you've caught me being predictable. A kettle is the first honest thing anyone's offered me tonight, and I'd hate to waste it."

She keeps her tail tucked and her eyes on the cabin door while she signals Ysolt with two slow fingers down by her hip: *wait.* "Mind if I bring my own cup? I'd like to hear what a woman with half the words offers for the other half."

entries.text:
Ashgrove laughs, a real laugh, bright and a little surprised. She steps back from the cabin door and sweeps the white glove toward the lamplight. "Bring your cup, by all means. I admire a guest who negotiates her own hospitality." The sentry's crossbow doesn't lower, but it stops tracking your heart and settles on your knees. On the far bank, in the reeds, nothing moves. Ysolt has seen your fingers.

The cabin is warm and low-beamed, smelling of tea, lamp-oil and wet rope. A kettle sits on a brazier, and a map of the river is pinned to the wall with a small iron pin at Marrowmere. Four raiders lounge at the walls with their weapons in easy reach. Ashgrove pours two cups with a steady hand and sits, gloved fingers folded around hers.

"Half the words, you say. Quite right. Sister Odalie has one half and you have the other, and I have a key, a hulk and eight nights. So we come to the part where one of you is clever enough to see that the river is going to be woken whether you like it or not." She pushes a cup toward you. "I'd rather it were woken *properly*, by someone who knows how to sing it back down afterwards. Isn't that the sort of offer you hear all the time, Miss Thorne? A person who's too sure of herself to say no?"

She's watching your tail.

Level up! New spell: Healing Word, since I've nearly died once already and a heal at range beats a prayer. No swaps, and I'll take the fixed 6 hit points, because I don't trust my luck with a d8 after that natural 1 at the hulk.

Then she holds up the key to the lantern light. "Corvin, drop us at Tanner's Stair by dawn. Ashgrove means to open the Weeping Locks at the new moon and drown the lower town, so I need Odalie, the Reeve, and a way to break that lock before then."

entries.text:
I need to correct myself before anything else. I made a mistake in my last message.

Your sheet shows that Vesper was already a level 2 bard when this game began, and she still is. I gave you the XP from the last scene, but 300 XP was never a level-up threshold for her. Level 3 needs 900 XP, and you have 425. There is no level-up to take right now, so Healing Word can't be chosen as a new spell. You already know it. Nothing on your sheet changes. I'm sorry for the confusion.

Here is where the sheet stands:
- You have 13 of 15 hit points, and all 3 first-level slots are spent (0/3).
- Your rapier is gone. The sentry took it off the barrel at the hulk, so you have your dagger and Vicious Mockery.
- The sheet lists "Garrow Quill's half of the sluice-pin", which I don't recognize and can't account for in the story so far. If it's your own addition from somewhere, tell me where it came from. Otherwise I'll treat it as something you picked up on the hulk and ask you how.

At level 3 you'd get the Lore college (three extra skills, Cutting Words, Expertise in two skills), a second spell level, and a new spell, so you're about 475 XP away.

The story still stands. The *Plump Heron* slides downriver through the small hours, and Tanner's Stair is a few hours off. You have the key and your wits, but no slots, and Ashgrove's flood is waiting at the Weeping Locks.
